attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

risks: THE BIG ONE: requirement 3 literally names `cd /output && rustc test18.rs` with NO --edition flag, and that compiles as EDITION 2015. If the port is written as idiomatic 2021 it will build under cargo and FAIL under bare rustc. Either (a) keep the source edition-agnostic so both work -- proven possible, /tmp/layout-poc2 builds clean under bare `rustc test18.rs` AND `cargo build --release` -- or (b) confirm the grader is allowed to pass `--edition 2021`. Recommendation: write edition-agnostic source so both are true simultaneously; that is strictly safer.

Edition-2015 landmines to avoid in the port even though they compile fine in 2021: never rely on disjoint-field closure capture (hard E0502 in 2015); never call `.into_iter()` on an array (silently yields &T in 2015 -- use `.iter()`, a for-loop, or `IntoIterator::into_iter(arr)`); always `use std::convert::TryFrom;` / `use std::iter::FromIterator;` explicitly since those are not in the 2015 prelude.

Overflow-check asymmetry between the two required build paths: bare `rustc test18.rs` has debug_assertions and overflow checks ON, `cargo build --release` has them OFF. Any arithmetic that can overflow (hash mixing, index math, i*2 for extreme n) will PANIC on the rustc binary and silently wrap on the cargo binary -- a byte-for-byte divergence between the project's own two builds. Use wrapping_mul/wrapping_add explicitly anywhere overflow is possible.

Performance asymmetry: bare `rustc test18.rs` is opt-level 0. The reference does n=200000 in 88ms; an unoptimized Rust build of an equivalent structure can be 10-30x slower. If any timing check exists it must be run against `rustc -O` or the cargo release binary, not the bare rustc output.

Mixing module-file conventions for the same module (both `sortedcontainers.rs` and `sortedcontainers/mod.rs`) is E0761 and kills BOTH build paths at once. Pick one and never leave a stray leftover file behind after refactoring.

Forgetting `edition = "2021"` in Cargo.toml makes cargo silently use 2015 -- so if you DO write 2021-only code, the cargo path breaks in exactly the same way as the rustc path, and the error message does not mention the edition.
Omitting the [[bin]] section is a manifest parse failure, so `cargo build --release` dies before compiling anything; and `path` must be `"test18.rs"` (root-relative), not `"src/test18.rs"`.

Stray warnings (e.g. dead_code from library modules that the entry file does not exercise) go to stderr, so they will not corrupt a stdout diff -- but they will appear in build logs on all three invocations. Add `#![allow(dead_code)]` (and consider `#![allow(unused_imports)]`) as the first line of test18.rs; an inner attribute on the crate root covers every submodule.

Do not put library modules under src/ while the entry file is at the root: rustc resolves `mod foo;` relative to the crate root file's directory, so src/foo.rs would be invisible to `mod foo;` in /output/test18.rs. Modules must be siblings of test18.rs.

/output will accumulate cargo artifacts (Cargo.lock, target/) alongside the rustc-built ./test18. These do not collide (verified by md5sum), but if anything downstream globs /output for executables it will see both /output/test18 and /output/target/release/test18, which are legitimately different binaries (different opt levels). Ensure any verification harness names the one it means.

risks: THE BIG ONE: requirement 3 literally names `cd /output && rustc test18.rs` with NO --edition flag, and that compiles as EDITION 2015. Idiomatic-2021 source will build under cargo and FAIL under bare rustc. Either (a) keep the source edition-agnostic so both paths work -- proven possible, /tmp/layout-poc2 builds clean and warning-free under bare `rustc test18.rs` AND `cargo build --release` -- or (b) confirm the grader may pass `--edition 2021`. Recommendation: write edition-agnostic source so both are simultaneously true.

Edition-2015 landmines to avoid in the port even though they compile fine in 2021: never rely on disjoint-field closure capture (hard E0502 in 2015); never call `.into_iter()` on an array (silently yields &T in 2015 -- use `.iter()`, a for-loop, or `IntoIterator::into_iter(arr)`); always write `use std::convert::TryFrom;` / `use std::iter::FromIterator;` explicitly since those are not in the 2015 prelude.

Overflow-check asymmetry between the two required build paths: bare `rustc test18.rs` has debug_assertions and overflow checks ON, `cargo build --release` has them OFF. Any arithmetic that can overflow (hash mixing, index math, i*2 at extreme n) PANICS on the rustc binary and wraps silently on the cargo binary -- a byte-for-byte divergence between the project's own two builds. Use wrapping_mul/wrapping_add explicitly wherever overflow is possible.

Performance asymmetry: bare `rustc test18.rs` is opt-level 0. The reference does n=200000 in 88ms; an unoptimized Rust build of an equivalent structure can be 10-30x slower. Any timing comparison must use `rustc -O` or the cargo release binary, not the bare rustc output.
Mixing module-file conventions for one module (leaving both `sortedcontainers.rs` and `sortedcontainers/mod.rs`) is E0761 and kills BOTH build paths at once -- easy to hit during refactoring.
Forgetting `edition = "2021"` in Cargo.toml makes cargo silently use 2015, so the cargo path breaks in exactly the same way as the rustc path, with an error message that never mentions editions.
Omitting the [[bin]] section is a manifest parse failure, and `path` must be `"test18.rs"` (root-relative), not `"src/test18.rs"`.

Do NOT put library modules under src/ while the entry file is at the root: rustc resolves `mod foo;` relative to the crate-root file's directory, so src/foo.rs is invisible to `mod foo;` in /output/test18.rs. Modules must be siblings of test18.rs.

Stray warnings (dead_code from library modules the entry file does not exercise) go to stderr so they cannot corrupt a stdout diff, but they appear in all build logs. Put `#![allow(dead_code)]` (and consider `#![allow(unused_imports)]`) as the first line of test18.rs -- an inner attribute on the crate root covers every submodule.

/output will accumulate cargo artifacts (Cargo.lock, target/) alongside the rustc-built ./test18. They do not collide (verified by md5sum), but /output/test18 and /output/target/release/test18 are legitimately DIFFERENT binaries with different opt levels and overflow-check settings, so any verification harness must name the one it means.
